name: Lunch Flow
tagline: An app for planning and coordinating lunches instead of relitigating the same decision every day at 12:05.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The planning core here is genuinely thin: a list of meals or options, a rotation or picker, a weekly view, and a shopping or prep list. An agent can hand you that in one sitting and it will work fine for one person on a laptop. Where it stops being a one-shot is everything around the core: a phone-first interface you actually reach for at 11:45, shared state for a household or a team, reminders that fire without you opening a tab, and any vendor or delivery integrations if the paid product leans on those. If the appeal is the decision engine, build it. If the appeal is that other humans see the same plan and get pinged about it, you are now maintaining a small sync product.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you keep a pool of lunch options, generate a week of them with rotation and constraint rules, edit the plan by hand, and export a consolidated shopping and prep list.
requirements: Node 20+ and a machine to run it on
A browser (mobile browser works, it just will not feel like an app)
Optional: a always-on box or cheap VPS if you want it reachable from your phone
whatYouLose: A polished mobile experience and home screen presence, you get a bookmark
Shared plans and voting for a household or an office, single-user local state is the default
Push notifications and reminders without a scheduler you set up yourself
Any built-in restaurant, vendor, or grocery integrations the paid product may offer
Someone else's curated meal or option library, you start with an empty table
moatNotes: Lunch decisions are a habit problem, not a data problem. Habit products win on friction and reminders, which is exactly the part a weekend build skips.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the hard part was never the rotation algorithm, it was showing up. A paid app is on the phone, nags at the right hour, and holds a plan that other people in the house or the office can see and argue with. A self-hosted version that lives on localhost gets used enthusiastically for nine days and then quietly stops existing, and $5 or $10 a month is a fair price for not having to be the person who maintains the nagging infrastructure.
notes: The build is easy, the habit is not. Consider whether you want software or a reminder.
prompt:
Build a local-first lunch planning web app called "Lunch Flow Lite". No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js (App Router) with TypeScript and Tailwind
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/lunchflow.db, schema created on first boot
- Server actions for all writes, no separate API layer, no ORM

Data model:
- option: id, name, kind (packed | cooked | bought | leftovers), effortMinutes, tags (csv), notes, active (bool), lastUsedOn (date, nullable)
- ingredient: id, optionId, name, quantity (free text)
- plan_entry: id, date (ISO), optionId (nullable), customText (nullable), locked (bool)

Features, in scope:
1. Options library: create, edit, archive. Filter by kind, tag, and max effort minutes.
2. Week view for the current week, Monday to Sunday, with a next/prev week control. Each day shows its planned option or a free-text entry.
3. "Fill week" button: assigns options to unlocked, empty days. Rules: never repeat an option within 10 days, respect a max effort setting stored in a settings row, prefer options with the oldest lastUsedOn, allow at most two "bought" entries per week. If constraints cannot be met, leave the day empty and say why.
4. Lock a day so refills skip it. Swap or clear any day inline.
5. Shopping and prep list for the visible week: merges ingredients across planned options, groups duplicates by name, shows quantities as a list under each name, and has checkboxes whose state is held in localStorage only.
6. Mark a day as eaten, which sets lastUsedOn on the option.
7. Export the week as Markdown to the clipboard.

Out of scope, do not build: auth, multi-user, sharing, push notifications, delivery or restaurant integrations, nutrition data, recipe scraping, calorie math, any external API calls.

Details:
- Mobile-width layout first, it will mostly be opened on a phone browser.
- Ship a seed script with 12 plausible lunch options and their ingredients so the app is not empty on first run.
- Any config goes in .env.example (just DB_PATH), never hardcode paths outside ./data.
- Add a README with install, seed, dev, and build commands, and a one-paragraph honest note that this has no reminders and no sync.
- Include vitest coverage for the fill-week rule engine specifically, nothing else.
